title: Theorem

\label{thm:equiv}
Let \( \pi \) be an irreducible supercuspidal representation of \( \mathrm{GL}_2(E) \). Then \( \pi \) is \( D^\times \)-distinguished if and only if \( \pi \) is \( \mathrm{GL}_2(F) \)-distinguished.

title: Remark
body_md:
The comparison in Theorem \ref{thm:equiv} is specific to supercuspidal representations and does not extend to all cuspidal representations. For example, suppose that \(\ell=2\) and that \(E/F\) is unramified. The special representation \(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi\), $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$ is cuspidal but not supercuspidal, and Theorems \ref{thm:principal} and \ref{thm:GL2} give
\[
\operatorname{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\mathbf1)=0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_2(F)}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\mathbf1)\ne0.
\]

label: coE
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{coE}
Let \(E/F\) be a quadratic extension of non-archimedean local fields of residue 
characteristic \(p\), and let \(\ell \neq p\) be a prime. Let \(q_E\) denote the 
cardinality of the residue field of \(E\). Then
\[
\dim_{\overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell}} \mathrm{H}^1(E^\times,\boldsymbol{1})
=
\begin{cases}
2, & \ell \mid q_E - 1, \\[4pt]
1, & \ell \nmid q_E - 1.
\end{cases}
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that $\mathrm{H}^1(E^\times,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{Hom}(E^\times,\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})$ and there is a standard decomposition
\[
E^\times \simeq \langle \pi_E \rangle \times \mathcal O_E^\times,
\qquad
\mathcal O_E^\times \simeq \boldsymbol{k}_E^\times \times (1 + \mathfrak p_E),
\]
where \(\pi_E\) is a uniformizer of \(E\), and \(\boldsymbol{k}_E \) 
is its residue field. Since \(\ell \neq p\), the pro-\(p\) group 
\(1 + \mathfrak p_E\) has no non-trivial homomorphism to \(\overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell}\). 
Hence
\[
\dim\ \mathrm{Hom}(E^\times, \overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell})
=
\dim\ \mathrm{Hom}(\langle \pi_E \rangle, \overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell})
+
\dim\ \mathrm{Hom}(\boldsymbol{k}_E^\times, \overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell}).
\]

The first factor is one-dimensional since \(\langle \pi_E \rangle \simeq \mathbb Z\). 
For the second factor, \(\boldsymbol{k}_E^\times\) is cyclic of order \(q_E - 1\), so its 
homomorphisms to \(\overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell}\) are non-zero exactly when 
\(\ell \mid q_E - 1\), in which case the space is one-dimensional. 
This finishes the proof.
head: environment

label: coEF
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{coEF}
With the same notations and assumptions as in Proposition \ref{coE}, we have

\[
\dim_{\overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell}} \mathrm{H}^1(E^\times/F^\times, \mathbf{1})
=
\begin{cases}
1, &\mbox{if }E/F \text{ is unramified} \text{ and } \ell \mid q + 1 , \\[4pt]
1, &\mbox{if } E/F \text{ is ramified} \text{ and } \ell = 2 , \\[4pt]
0, & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
where $q$ denote the cardinality of the residue field of $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have \(\mathrm{H}^1(E^\times/F^\times, \mathbf{1}) = \operatorname{Hom}(E^\times/F^\times, \overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell})\).
If $E/F$ is an unramified quadratic extension, $E^\times/F^\times$ is the direct product of the cyclic group $C_{q+1}$ of order $q+1$ and a pro-$p$ group. Then $$\mathrm{Hom}(E^\times/F^\times,\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})=\mathrm{Hom}(C_{q+1},\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})$$ since $\ell\neq p$ and the dimension is 1 if and only if $\ell|q+1$.

If $E/F$ is a ramified quadratic extension, when $p\neq2$, $E^\times/F^\times$ is the direct product of the cyclic group $C_2$ of order 2 and a pro-$p$ group. Then $\mathrm{Hom}(E^\times/F^\times,\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})=\mathrm{Hom}(C_{2},\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})$ and the dimension is 1 if and only if $\ell=2$. When $p=2$, $E^\times/F^\times$ is a pro-$2$ group so $\mathrm{Hom}(E^\times/F^\times, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})=0$ since $\ell\neq 2$.

This proves the formula.

body_md:
\label{cofinite}
    Suppose $G$ is a finite $p$-group, i.e., its order $|G|$ is a power of $p$, $A$ is a discrete $\ell$-torsion $G$-module and $\ell\neq p$. Then $\mathrm{H}^r(G,A)=0$ for $r\geq 1$.

label: copro-p
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{copro-p}
    Suppose $G$ is a pro-$p$ group, $A$ is a discrete $\ell$-torsion $G$-module and $\ell\neq p$. Then $\mathrm{H}^r(G,A)=0$ for $r\geq 1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: According to \cite[Proposition 4.2]{milneCFT}, we have $\mathrm{H}^r(G,A)=\lim\limits_{\longrightarrow}\mathrm{H}^r(G/H,A^H)$ as $H$ runs through the open normal subgroups of $G$. Since $G$ is a pro-$p$ group, $G/H$ is a finite $p$-group and $A^H\subset A$ is also a discrete $\ell$-torsion $G/H$-module. Using Proposition \ref{cofinite}, $\mathrm{H}^r(G/H,A^H)=0$. Then $\mathrm{H}^r(G,A)=0$ for $r\geq 1$.

title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Key lemma

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
         \item 
         Note that $\mathrm{Ext}_{D^\times}^1(\boldsymbol{1},\chi\circ\det)=\mathrm{H}^1(D^\times,\chi\circ\det)$. There exists a short sequence:
         \begin{align*}
             1\longrightarrow Z\longrightarrow D^\times\longrightarrow PD^\times\longrightarrow 1
         \end{align*}
         By the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence, we have
         \begin{align*}\label{f1}
             0\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,(\chi\circ\det)^{Z})\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(D^\times,\chi\circ\det)\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(Z,(\chi\circ\det))^{PD^\times}.\tag{3-1}
         \end{align*}
         Consider $(\chi\circ\det)^{Z}$. For any $v\in (\chi\circ\det)^{Z}$ and $z\in Z$, we have $$z\cdot v=\chi(\det(z))v=\chi^2(z)v=v.$$
         Hence $(\chi\circ\det)^{Z}$ is vanishing if and only if $\chi^2\neq\boldsymbol{1}$.\\

         When $\chi^2\neq\boldsymbol{1}$, $\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,(\chi\circ\det)^{Z})=0$. For $\mathrm{H}^1(Z,\chi\circ\det)$, given $\varphi\in\mathrm{H}^1(Z,\chi\circ\det)$, $\varphi$ satisfies $\varphi(z_1z_2)=\chi^2(z_1)\varphi(z_2)+\varphi(z_1),z_1,z_2\in F^\times.$ Because $\varphi(z_1z_2)=\varphi(z_2z_1),$ we have $$\chi^2(z_1)\varphi(z_2)+\varphi(z_1)=\chi^2(z_2)\varphi(z_1)+\varphi(z_2).$$ Then $\chi^2\neq \boldsymbol{1}$ implies the existence of $z_0$ which satisfies $\chi^2(z_0)\neq1$. Fix $z_1=z_0$. Therefore, $\forall z_2\in F^\times$, $\varphi(z_2)=(\chi^2(z_2)-1)\dfrac{\varphi(z_0)}{\chi^2(z_0)-1}$, and so $\varphi$ is a coboundry. Then $\mathrm{H}^1(Z,(\chi\circ\det))=0$ and so $\mathrm{H}^1(D^\times,\chi\circ\det)=0$.\\
\item 
         When $\chi^2=\boldsymbol{1}$ but $\chi\neq\boldsymbol{1}$, $\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,(\chi\circ\det)^{Z})=\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,\chi\circ\det).$ Let $O_D$ be the valuation ring of $D$, $\mathfrak{p}_D$ be its unique maximal ideal and $\boldsymbol{k}_D\cong \mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ be its residual field. We define
         \begin{align*}
             U:=O_D^\times Z/Z\cong O_D^\times/O_F^\times,\quad  U_1:=(1+\mathfrak{p}_D)Z/Z\cong1+\mathfrak{p}_D/1+\mathfrak{p}_F.
         \end{align*}
         Then $U/U_1=\boldsymbol{k}_D^\times/\boldsymbol{k}_F^\times\cong C_{q+1}$ which is a cyclic group of order $q+1$. There exists a short sequence:
         \begin{align*}
             1\longrightarrow U\longrightarrow PD^\times \stackrel{\mu}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow1
         \end{align*}
         where $\mu$ is the exponential valuation on $D^\times$. Therefore, for $PD^\times/U_1$, we have 
         \begin{align*}
             1\longrightarrow U/U_1\longrightarrow PD^\times/U_1 \stackrel{\bar{\mu}}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow1.
         \end{align*}
         We claim that the group $PD^\times/U_1$ is isomorphic to the dihedral group $D_{2(q+1)}=C_{q+1}\rtimes C_2$. Actually we just need to prove the existence of the section $s:\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow PD^\times/U_1$ such that $\bar{\mu}\circ s=\mathrm{id}.$ We define 
         \begin{align*}
             s:\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow PD^\times/U_1,\quad s(0)=1,s(1)=\bar{\Pi}
         \end{align*}
         where $\Pi$ is the prime element of $O_D$ and $\bar{\Pi}$ is the image of $\Pi Z$ in $PD^\times/U_1$. Then $s$ is a homomorphism and $\bar{\mu}\circ s=\mathrm{id}$.

         Now we have the exact sequence of groups:
        \begin{align*}
            1\longrightarrow U_1\longrightarrow PD^\times\longrightarrow D_{2(q+1)}\longrightarrow1.
        \end{align*}
        By the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence, we have
        \begin{align*}\label{f2}
            0\longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)},(\chi\circ\det)^{U_1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,\chi\circ\det)\longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(U_1,\chi\circ\det)^{D_{2(q+1)}}.\tag{3-2}
        \end{align*}
        Since $U_1$ is a pro-$p$ group, $\chi$ is a quadratic character and $p\neq 2$, $\chi\circ\det$ is trivial on $U_1$ and $$\mathrm{H}^1(U_1,\chi\circ\det)=\mathrm{Hom}(U_1,\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})=0.$$ Then 
        $\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,\chi\circ\det)= \mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)},(\chi\circ\det)^{U_1})= \mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)},\chi\circ\det)$. By the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence, one has the following exact sequence
        \begin{align*}\label{f3}
            0\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(C_2,(\chi\circ\det)^{C_{q+1}})\longrightarrow \mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)},\chi\circ\det)\\\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^1(C_{q+1},\chi\circ\det)^{C_2}\longrightarrow\mathrm{H}^2(C_2,(\chi\circ\det)^{C_{q+1}})\tag{3-3}
        \end{align*}
        
        If $\chi\circ\det|_{C_{q+1}}\neq\boldsymbol{1}$, given any $ a \in (\chi\circ\det)^{C_{q+1}}$ and $r\in C_{q+1}$, we have $$r\cdot a=\chi\circ\det(r)a=a,$$ which implies that $a$ must be zero. Then $\mathrm{H}^1(C_2,(\chi\circ\det)^{C_{q+1}})$=0. Since $C_{q+1}$ is a cyclic group and $\chi\circ\det|_{C_{q+1}}\neq\boldsymbol{1}$, $\mathrm{H}^1(C_{q+1},\chi\circ\det)$=0. In this case, we have $\mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)},\chi\circ\det)$=0.

        If $\chi\circ\det|_{C_{q+1}}=\boldsymbol{1}$, 
        then $\chi\circ\det|_{C_2}\neq\boldsymbol{1}$. Otherwise $\chi$ is trivial,  contradicting the condition that $\chi\neq\mathbf{1}$. In this case, 
        \begin{equation}\label{first:van}\mathrm{H}^1(C_2,(\chi\circ\det)^{C_{q+1}})=\mathrm{H}^1(C_2,\chi\circ\det)=0\tag{3-4}\end{equation} since $C_2$ is also a cyclic group and $\chi\circ\det|_{C_2}\neq\boldsymbol{1}$. It remains to determine $\mathrm{H}^1(C_{q+1}, \chi \circ \det)^{C_2}.$
Since \(C_{q+1}\) acts trivially on the coefficient module \(\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}\), we have that
$$
\mathrm{H}^1(C_{q+1}, \chi \circ \det) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}).$$

For \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})\) and \(s \in C_2\) of order $2$, the action of \(C_2\) is given by
\[
(s \cdot f)(r) = (\chi \circ \det)(s)f(s^{-1} r s)=(\chi \circ \det)(s)f(r^{-1})= -(\chi \circ \det)(s) f(r), \quad \forall r \in C_{q+1}.
\]
Because \(\chi \circ \det|_{C_2} \neq \boldsymbol{1}\), we have$(\chi \circ \det)(s) = -1.$
Therefore, $(s \cdot f)(r) = f(r)$
and so every \(f \in \mathrm{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})\) is invariant under \(C_2\). Hence
$\operatorname{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})^{C_2}
= \operatorname{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}).$
Now we distinguish two cases: $\ell\nmid\ q+1$ and $\ell|\ q+1$.
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt]
\item If \(\ell \nmid q+1\), then for any \(f \in \operatorname{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})\), we have
$(q+1) f(r) = f(r^{q+1}) = f(1) = 0$
which implies \(f(r) = 0\). Thus
$\operatorname{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}) = 0$
and consequently
\[
H^1(D_{2(q+1)}, \chi \circ \det) = 0.
\]

\item If \(\ell \mid q+1\), then \(\operatorname{Hom}(C_{q+1}, \overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})\) is a one-dimensional \(\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}\)-vector space.
Moreover, in the case when \(\ell \mid q+1\) and \(\chi \circ \det|_{C_2} \neq \boldsymbol{1}\), 
we have \(M = \overline{\boldsymbol F_\ell}\) with \(C_2\) acting via
$$s \cdot m = (\chi \circ \det)(s) \, m = -m, \forall m \in M.$$
Since \(\ell \neq 2\), we have
\[
M^{C_2} = \{ m \in M \mid m = -m \} = 0.
\]
For the cyclic group \(C_2\), the standard cohomology formula gives the following isomorphism
\[
\mathrm{H}^2(C_2, M) \cong \mathrm{H}_T^0(C_2,M)= M^{C_2} / (1 + s)M.
\]
where $\mathrm{H_T^0(C_2,M)}$ denotes the Tate cohommology group (see \cite[Section 2]{milneCFT}).  Since \(M^{C_2} = 0\), it follows immediately that
$\mathrm{H}^2(C_2, M) = 0.$
Thus, by the spectral sequence (\ref{f3})
the last term $\mathrm{H}^2(C_2,(\chi\circ\det)^{C_{q+1}})$ vanishes. Together with \eqref{first:van}, it forces that
\[
\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)}, \chi\circ\det)=\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{H}^1(C_{q+1},\chi\circ\det)^{C_2}=\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}(C_{q+1},\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}) = 1.
\]
\end{itemize}

            

        For $\mathrm{H}^1(Z,(\chi\circ\det))^{PD^\times}$, it equals $\mathrm{Hom}(Z,\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})^{PD^\times}$ due to the fact that $\chi^2=\boldsymbol{1}$. Then given any $f
        \in \mathrm{Hom}(Z,\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})$ and $a\in PD^\times$, $$a\cdot f(z)=\chi\circ\det(a)f(z)=f(z). $$ Since $\chi\circ\det$ is not trivial, $f=0$ which means $\mathrm{H}^1(Z,(\chi\circ\det))^{PD^\times}=0$ . 
        
    In a short summary, when $\chi^2=\boldsymbol{1}$ but $\chi\neq\boldsymbol{1}$,
    \begin{align*}
        \mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Ext}_{D^\times}^1(\boldsymbol{1},\chi\circ\det)=\begin{cases}
            1,\ \mathrm{if}\ \chi\circ\det|_{C_{q+1}}=\boldsymbol{1}\ \mathrm{and}\ \ell|q+1;\\
            0,\ \mathrm{others.}
        \end{cases}
    \end{align*}\\
\item 
        When $\chi=\boldsymbol{1}$, we have $\mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}^1(\boldsymbol{1},\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,\boldsymbol{1})$. By the exact sequence (\ref{f2}), $\mathrm{H}^1(U_1,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Then
        \begin{align*}
\mathrm{H}^1(PD^\times,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{H}^1(D_{2(q+1)},\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{Hom}(D_{2(q+1)},\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})=\mathrm{Hom}(D_{2(q+1)}^{ab},\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell})
        \end{align*}
    where $D_{2(q+1)}^{ab}\cong C_2\times C_2$ is the  Abelianization of $D_{2(q+1)}$. Since $\ell\neq 2$, it is zero.
     \end{enumerate}This finishes the proof.

label: prop:Cq+1
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:Cq+1}
    Let $\chi$ be a quadratic character of $F^\times$. Then $\chi\circ\det$ is trivial on $k_D^\times/k_F^\times\cong C_{q+1}$ if and only if $\chi$ is trivial on $k_F^\times$, where $k_D$(resp. $k_F$) denotes the residue field of $D$(resp. $F$).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that from the proof of Lemma \ref{3.3}(2), $C_{q+1} \cong k_D^\times / k_F^\times$, 
where $k_D \cong \mathbb F_{q^2}$ and $ k_F \cong \mathbb F_q $. 
The determinant map $ \det : D^\times \to F^\times $ is given by the reduced norm
$\mathrm{Nrd} : D^\times \to F^\times,$
which induces a surjection on residue fields $k_D^\times \twoheadrightarrow k_F^\times.$ Hence the restriction of $ \chi \circ \det $ to $ C_{q+1} $ is trivial if and only if 
$\chi$ is trivial on $k_F^\times$.

label: coro:ramified character
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{coro:ramified character}
    If $\chi$ is a quadratic ramified character of $F^\times$, then $\chi\circ\det$ is not trivial on $C_{q+1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose that \(\chi \circ \det\) is trivial on \(C_{q+1}\). By Proposition \ref{prop:Cq+1}, \(\chi\) is trivial on \(k_F^\times\). Moreover, since \(\chi\) is a quadratic character and \(1+\mathfrak{p}_F\) is a pro-\(p\) group with \(p \neq 2\), \(\chi\) must be trivial on \(1+\mathfrak{p}_F\). Consequently, \(\chi\) is trivial on \(\mathcal{O}_F^\times\), which contradicts the assumption that \(\chi\) is a ramified character of \(F^\times\).

title: Proof
body_md:
\
    \newline
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Assume $q_E^2\not\equiv1(\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)$. If $ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\pi(\chi\nu^{1/2},\chi\nu^{-1/2}),\boldsymbol{1})\neq 0$, by Lemma \ref{3.2}, we have $\chi\chi^{\sigma}=\boldsymbol{1}$. Then $\chi|_{F^\times}\circ \mathrm{Nm}_{E/F}=\boldsymbol{1}$ which implies $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}_{F^\times}$ or $\omega_{E/F}$  (see \cite[Lemma 4.2]{cui2024}). At this time, the central character of $\pi$ restricting to the center $Z(D^\times)$ is trivial and so  $\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$.
         \begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt]
             \item If $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$, $\chi\circ\det$ factors through $D^\times\rightarrow PD^\times$. Taking the functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(-,\boldsymbol{1})$, we have
         \begin{align*}
             0\longrightarrow&\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\pi(\chi\nu^{1/2},\chi\nu^{-1/2}),\boldsymbol{1})\\&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\mathrm{St}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ext}^1_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})
         \end{align*}
         and dim $\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=1$.
         Due to Lemma \ref{3.3}(3) that $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$, then $\mathrm{St}_\chi$ is not distinguished.
         \item If $\chi|_{F^\times}=\omega_{E/F}$, we have $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Since $q_E^2\not\equiv1\pmod\ell,\ell\nmid (q_E+1)$. By Lemma \ref{3.3}(2), $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Therefore, by the exact sequence \eqref{exactsequence St}, $\mathrm{St}_\chi$ is  distinguished and $\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{St}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$.
         \end{itemize}

If $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\pi(\chi\nu^{1/2},\chi\nu^{-1/2})=0$, we can consider another exact sequence
\begin{align*}
    0\longrightarrow\chi\circ\det\longrightarrow\pi(\chi\nu^{-1/2},\chi\nu^{1/2})\longrightarrow\mathrm{St}_\chi\longrightarrow0
\end{align*}
Taking the functor $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(-,\boldsymbol{1})$, we have $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{St}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=0$ i.e. $\mathrm{St}_\chi$ is not distinguished.
\item 
Suppose $q_E\equiv1(\mathrm{mod\ \ell)}$. Then $\nu$ is trivial and
\[\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})=\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\chi,\boldsymbol{1})+\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{St}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1}). \]
         Suppose that $ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})\neq 0$. If $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$, then $\mathrm{St}_\chi$ is not distinguished. If $\chi|_{F^\times}=\omega_{E/F}$, 
       then $\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{St}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$. Moreover, if $\pi$ is not distinguished, $\mathrm{St}_\chi$ is also not distinguished.
         \\
\item 
         Suppose that $q_E\equiv-1(\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)$. When $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\pi(\chi\nu^{1/2},\chi\nu^{-1/2}),\boldsymbol{1})\neq0$, assuming $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$, by a similar argument to the case $q_E^2\not\equiv1(\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)$, $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Then  $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=0$, i.e. $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is not distinguished by the exact sequence \eqref{f35}.
         
         Suppose that $\chi|_{F^\times}=\omega_{E/F}$. If $E/F$ is unramified, $q_E=q^2$ and $\ell|q^2+1$ then $\ell\nmid q+1$. Otherwise $\ell|2q$, contradicting $\ell\neq2$ and  $\ell\neq p$. By Lemma \ref{3.3}(2), $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Therefore, followed by the exact sequence \eqref{f34}, $\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$. For the exact sequence \eqref{f35}), consider $(\chi\circ\det)\nu_2|_{D^\times}$. Denote by $\nu_F$ the absolute value of $F^\times$ and $\nu=\nu_F\circ \mathrm{Nm}_{E/F}$. Given any $ g\in D^\times$,$$(\chi\circ\det)\nu_2(g)=\chi(\det(g))|\det(g)|_E=\chi(\det(g))|\det(g)|_F^2=(\chi\cdot\nu_F^2)\circ\det(g).$$ Since $q^2\equiv-1(\mathrm{mod}\ \ell),\ \nu_F^2=\omega_{E/F}$. In this case $\chi|_{F^\times}\cdot\nu_F^2=\omega_{E/F}^2=\boldsymbol{1}_{F^\times}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}((\chi\circ\det)\nu_2,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\boldsymbol{1},\boldsymbol{1})$ with dimension 1. Then we will prove $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\boldsymbol{1},\boldsymbol{1})$ is surjective.

         Actually, since the central character restricting to the center $Z(D^\times)$ is trivial, we can rewrite the exact sequence \eqref{f35} in the category of smooth representations of $PD^\times$:
         \begin{align*}
             0\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\boldsymbol{1},\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}^1(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1}).
         \end{align*}
         Followed by Proposition \ref{extfix}, $$\mathrm{Ext}^1_{PD^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})\cong\mathrm{Ext}_{D_{2(q+1)}}^1((\mathrm{Sp}_\chi)^{U_1},\boldsymbol{1})$$ where $U_1=(1+\mathfrak{p}_D)F^\times/F^\times$. Since $\ell\nmid 2(q+1)$, Maschke's Theorem implies the group algebra $\overline{\boldsymbol{F}_\ell}[D_{2(q+1)}]$ is semisimple. Then $\mathrm{Ext}_{D_{2(q+1)}}^1((\mathrm{Sp}_\chi)^{U_1},\boldsymbol{1})=0$ i.e. $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\boldsymbol{1},\boldsymbol{1})$ is surjective.

         Therefore, $\dim \mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi, \boldsymbol{1})=0$, i.e., $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is not distinguished.\\

         If $E/F$ is ramified, $q_E=q$ and so $\ell|q+1$. In this case, the quadratic character $\chi|_{F^\times}=\omega_{E/F}$ is ramified. Then Corollary \ref{coro:ramified character} implies $\chi\circ\det|_{C_{q+1}}$ is not trivial. Followed by Lemma \ref{3.3}(2), one has $\mathrm{Ext}_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Now, by the exact sequence \eqref{f34}, $\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$. Thanks to the fact that $q=q_E\equiv-1(\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)$, $q^2\equiv1(\mathrm{mod}\ \ell)$ then $\nu_F^2$ is trivial and 
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}((\chi\circ\det)\nu_2,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}((\chi\cdot\nu_F^2)\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0.
\end{align*}
By the exact sequence \eqref{f35},  $\mathrm{dim}\ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$ and so $\mathrm{Sp_\chi}$ is distinguished.\\

If $\pi$ is not distinguished by $D^\times$, Lemma \ref{3.2} implies $\chi\chi^\sigma\neq\boldsymbol{1}$ i.e., $\chi|_{F^\times}\not\in\{\boldsymbol{1},\omega_{E/F}\}$.

Suppose $E/F$ is unramified. Then $q_E=q^2$ and $\ell\nmid\ q+1$. By Lemma \ref{3.3}(2), $\mathrm{Ext}^1_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$ which implies $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Then $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is not distinguished followed by the exact sequence \eqref{f35}.

Suppose $E/F$ is ramified. Then $q=q_E$ and $\ell|q+1$. The central character of $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is $\chi^2$. If $\chi^2|_{F^\times}\neq\boldsymbol{1}$, $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ must be not distinguished. Thus we only need to consider the case $\chi^2|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$ with $\chi|_{F^\times}\not\in\{\boldsymbol{1},\omega_{E/F}\}$. Since the central character restricting to the center $Z(D^\times)$ is trivial, we can reduce the exact sequence \eqref{f34} to those representations of $PD^\times$:
\begin{align*}
             0\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(\pi(\chi\nu^{1/2},\chi\nu^{-1/2}),\boldsymbol{1})\\
             \longrightarrow \mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ext}^1_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})\longrightarrow\mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}^1(\pi(\chi\nu^{1/2},\chi\nu^{-1/2}),\boldsymbol{1}).  
\end{align*}
If $\chi|_{F^\times}$ is a ramified quadratic character, $\mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=\mathrm{Ext}_{D^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=0$ by Corollary \ref{coro:ramified character} and Lemma \ref{3.3}(2). Then $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is not distinguished. 

If $\chi|_{F^\times}$ is an unramified quadratic character, then Proposition \ref{prop:Cq+1} shows that $\chi\circ\det$ is trivial on $C_{q+1}$. Thus dim $\mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=1$ by Lemma \ref{3.3}(2) and Lemma \ref{l4.2} implies $\mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}^1(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})=0$. Therefore, $$\dim\ \mathrm{Hom}_{PD^\times}(J_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=\dim\ \mathrm{Ext}_{PD^\times}^1(\chi\circ\det,\boldsymbol{1})=1.$$ Followed by
the exact sequence \eqref{f35} and the fact that $\mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}((\chi\circ\det)\nu_2,\boldsymbol{1})=0$, $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is distinguished and $\dim\ \mathrm{Hom}_{D^\times}(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi,\boldsymbol{1})=1$.

Therefore, when $\pi$ is not distinguished, $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is distinguished if and only if $E/F$ is ramified and $\chi|_{F^\times}$ is an unramified quadratic character.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent This finishes the proof.

label: c3.1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{c3.1}
        Let $\pi$ be an irreducible supercuspidal representation of $\mathrm{GL}_2(E)$. Then $\pi$ is $D^\times$-distinguished if and only if $\pi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished. (Here $\ell$ is arbitary except $\ell=p$)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Followed by \cite[Theorem 3.4]{KM20}, for either $H=D^\times$ or $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$, an integral supercuspidal $\overline{\mathbb Q_{\ell}}$-representation
$\widetilde\pi$ satisfies that if $\widetilde\pi$ is $H$-distinguished, then $r_\ell(\widetilde\pi)$ is $H-$distinguished where $r_\ell(\widetilde\pi)$ is the reduction modulo $\ell$ of $\widetilde\pi$.

Suppose $\pi$ is $D^\times$-distinguished. Since $D^\times$ is a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_2(E)$, \cite[Theorem 3.4]{cui2024} implies that if $\pi$ is $D^\times$-distinguished. Then there exists a $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_\ell}$-lift $\widetilde{\pi}$ of $\pi$ such that it is supercuspidal and distinguished by $D^\times$. Note that $\tilde{\pi}$ is $D^\times$-distinguished if and only if $\tilde{\pi}$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished by \cite[Theorem C]{prased1992}. Then $\pi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished since $\pi$ is the reduction modulo $\ell$ of $\widetilde\pi$.

Conversely, suppose $\pi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished. Because $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$ is also closed in $\mathrm{GL}_2(E)$, by a similar argument as before,  we have $\pi$ is $D^\times$-distinguished.

title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem \ref{c3.1}, $\pi$ is $D^\times$-distinguished if and only if $\pi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item 
The case $\ell=2$ is \cite[Theorem 10.8]{vincent2019}.  
\item 
Assume $\ell\neq2$.
 
Suppose $m=1$, $T/T_0$ and $\mathcal D/\mathcal D_0$ must be ramified or unramified at the same time. Followed by \cite[Theorem 10.9,(3)]{vincent2019}, $\pi$ is distinguished if and only if $\delta_0$ is trivial. 

Now suppose $m=2$. Followed by \cite[Proposition 9.8]{vincent2019}, $T/T_0$ is ramified; otherwise $m$ will be odd. Moreover, \cite[Remark 10.10]{vincent2019} implies $\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}_0$ is unramified. Then \cite[Theorem 10.9,(2)]{vincent2019} shows that $\pi$ is distinguished if and only if $\delta_0=\omega_{\mathcal D/\mathcal D_0}$.
\end{enumerate}
This finishes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Followed by the exact sequence \eqref{f51}:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item If $\chi_1|_{F^\times}\neq 1$ and $\chi_2|_{F^\times}\neq 1$, by Lemma \ref{l51}, $\mathrm{Ext}_{F^\times\times F^\times}^1(\chi_1\boxtimes\chi_2,\boldsymbol{1})=0$, then $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_2(F)}(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})\cong\mathrm{Hom}_{E^\times}(\chi_1\chi_2^\sigma,\boldsymbol{1})$. Therefore, $\pi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished if and only if $\chi_1\chi_2^\sigma=\boldsymbol{1}$.
        \item If just one of the two characters $\chi_1|_{F^\times},\chi_2|_{F^\times}$ is $\boldsymbol{1}$, then $\mathrm{Hom}_{F^\times \times F^\times} (\chi_1 \boxtimes \chi_2, \mathbf{1})=\mathrm{Hom}_{E^\times} (\chi_1 \chi_2^\sigma, \mathbf{1})=0$, and so $\pi$ is not $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished.
        \item If $\chi_1|_{F^\times}=\chi_2|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$, dim $\mathrm{Hom}_{F^\times \times F^\times} (\chi_1 \boxtimes \chi_2, \mathbf{1})=1$, and so $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{GL}_2(F)}(\pi,\boldsymbol{1})\neq 0$ i.e. $\pi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished.
    \end{enumerate}
    This finishes the proof.

label: spl=2
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{spl=2} Assume $\ell=2$. Then
    $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished if and only if $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Recall that $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is a subquotient representation of $\pi(\chi,\chi)$ and that it is cuspidal. According to \cite[Theorem 1.3]{vin2026}, $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished if and only if $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is $\sigma$-selfdual. 
   
   Note that
        $(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi)^\vee\simeq\mathrm{Sp}_{\chi^{-1}}$ and  $(\mathrm{Sp}_\chi)^\sigma\simeq\mathrm{Sp}_{\chi^\sigma}$. 
         When $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is $\sigma$-selfdual, comparing the central characters, we have $(\chi^{-1})^2=(\chi^\sigma)^2$ then $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$ since $\ell=2$. Conversely, when $\chi|_{F^\times}=\boldsymbol{1}$, $\mathrm{Sp}_\chi$ is $\sigma$-selfdual and so it is $\mathrm{GL}_2(F)$-distinguished.
